items.title: October 2026 Rental Report: Rents Rise Annually for the First Time Since June 2023
items.description: October 2026 Rental Report: Rents Rise Annually for the First Time Since June 2023 By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Nov 18, 2026 Highlights October 2026 marks the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023. The change was modest with the median asking rent rising by just $1 (+0.1%) from October 2025 to $1,692. Rents continue to split the difference between their recent highs and prepandemic level. They are down $82 (-4.6%) from summer 2022 peak, and up $221 (+15%) from pre-pandemic level. Rent rebounded in larger units, while studio rents continue to soften: Studio: $1,411, down $17 (-1.2%) YoY 1-bed: $1,566, up $1(+0.1%) YoY 2-bed: $1,889, up $5 (+0.3%) YoY In 2026Q3, multifamily deliveries have returned to pre-pandemic levels as the 2021–2022 boom cohorts clear. Looking ahead, a cooling in starts suggests that new rental supply is likely to stay modest in the near term. Completions: 330,000, down 26% YoY Under Construction: 674,000, down 2.7% YoY Starts: 403,000, down 9.2% YoY All U.S. regions share the national pattern of cooling completions but differ in what comes next based on starts and the under-construction pipeline: the Northeast is rebuilding, the Midwest and South are easing from elevated levels, and the West looks the most likely to tighten. In October 2026, the median asking rent rose 0.1% year over year, the first annual increase since June 2023. Median asking rent for 0–2 bedroom properties across the 50 largest metro areas was $1,692, about $221 (15%) above the pre-pandemic level but $82 (-4.6%) below the August 2022 peak. Median asking rents fell year over year for more than three years, and the 2021–2022 multifamily construction boom was the main driver of the decline. Projects started in those years were delivered in 2023–2025 and added supply that held rents down. According to the Housing Vacancy Survey, the rental vacancy rate reached 7.6% in 2026Q3, the highest level since early 2014. However, as construction activity unwinds, the downward pressure on rents from new supply has eased. At the same time, elevated borrowing costs may be supporting rental demand by keeping more households renting. The path ahead largely depends on whether new multifamily deliveries remain strong enough to outpace that demand. Larger units see rents increase In October 2026, the median asking rent for two-bedroom units rose 0.3% year over year, the first annual increase since May 2023. At $1,889, the national median for two-bedroom units is $82 (4.2%) below its July 2022 peak. Even after more than three years of softness, it remains $299 (18.8%) above its level seven years ago. The rent for one-bedroom units increased 0.1% in October 2026 on a year over year basis, and now stands at $1,566. This was the first month of annual rent growth since June 2023. Rent was $95 (-5.7%) lower than the peak observed during August 2022, but still $191 (13.9%) higher than in October 2019. In October 2026, the median asking rent for studios fell by 1.2%, marking the 39th consecutive month of annual declines. The median rent of studios was $1,411 in October, down by $73 (-4.9%) from its peak, seen in Fall 2022. Nevertheless, the median asking rent for studios was still $141 (11.1%) higher than seven years ago. During this period, the newly completed units boosted the total rental stock by 3.2%, or a rate of more than 1% per year. This surge in deliveries was largely driven by the multifamily starts boom of 2021–2023, when 1,452,000 units were started (an average of 484,000 per year), 33% more than in 2017–2019. Because projects typically take about 1.5 years to complete , those starts translated into the wave of completions in 2023–2025. items.title: BTR Operators Push For Treasury To Loosen Rules As Consolidation Looms
items.description: The build-to-rent sector is facing a second round of wrangling with the government after a hard-fought battle with lawmakers over the summer to keep the industry from facing steep regulations as part of the housing bill that made its way through Congress . BTR operators and industry advocates are pushing for changes to proposed rules from the Department of the Treasury that will dictate how the restrictions on BTR operators from the 21st Century Road to Housing Act are implemented. Operators in the sector say the rules could hamper new development and, regardless of what’s adjusted, expect consolidation to sweep across the sector. “Hopefully that gets adjusted, because that will have a severe impact on capital flows and ultimately the building of new homes and new rental communities,” Richard Ross , CEO of Atlanta-based Quinn Residences , said of the proposed rules. Unsplash/Michael Tuszynski The proposed regulations require large institutional investors, which are defined in the original legislation as firms with at least 350 single-family rental units, to adopt written BTR programs before they purchase a community and would preclude BTR operators from purchasing properties more than 18 months after the home received its certificate of occupancy. Ross, whose firm has developed or purchased 5,200 homes across 34 communities since its founding in 2020, wrote in a letter submitted as a public comment to Treasury that it can frequently take two years or more to stabilize a newly built community. The two new rules would make it more difficult for homebuilders to sell excess inventory to build-to-rent operators, hampering activity in a pool of properties that BTR operators have long dipped into, Ross told Bisnow . His letter was one of more than 100 public comments filed so far. Other operators and industry groups, including the nonpartisan trade association National Rental Home Council , are still crafting their own submissions, CEO Adrianne Todman said. The public comment period closes on Nov. 23. “The Treasury Department has put forward some thoughtful rules where they're trying to thread the needle very carefully by making sure they are properly implementing the legislative ban on investors being able to buy homes but also making sure that it's not having any detrimental impacts to the housing marketplace and particularly the rental marketplace,” Todman said. The push to shift the rules follows the first bout of uncertainty that shrouded the BTR sector when the Road to Housing legislation was originally being debated. The bill debuted with strict restrictions on the BTR business model that threatened to upend the sector. It took intense lobbying for the rules to shift. Investment in the sector was severely scaled back during that debate, as investors waited to see what the final legislation would include. “When there was a threat to being able to build new rental supply via build-to-rent, we saw that there was millions of dollars and thousands of units that went on the sidelines and that those resources were frozen,” Todman said. “Those resources are thawing out a bit, and we want to make sure that they thaw out even more.” The push for clear guidelines gained new momentum after Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections. Some senators-elect ran on campaigns explicitly against corporate ownership of homes, including James Talarico in Texas and Josh Turek in Iowa. Talarico’s website includes a call to “ban Wall Street from buying up housing stock to enrich wealthy investors while making it harder for families to afford homes,” and Turek’s platform includes a call to ban private equity firms from purchasing single-family homes. The Road to Housing legislation adds new compliance standards and an element of federal oversight, including public reporting requirements for large operators, that are expected to lead to a wave of buyouts and mergers across the sector. The consolidation is likely coming regardless of where Treasury lands on its rules, as smaller players are squeezed by costs that large operators that benefit from economies of scale can more easily absorb. “You put it all together, it's just a tougher backdrop for them to really justify their existence,” said Haendel St. Juste , equity research analyst at Mizuho , who upgraded the two major publicly traded single-family rental firms to outperform in September. Unsplash/Nate Johnston New compliance costs for operators with at least 350 units but not thousands will raise operating costs for smaller BTR firms around the same time that the private equity funds backing those platforms reach the end of their lives. A substantial amount of the debt backing private BTR and SFR firms was issued around five to seven years ago and is reaching the end of its natural life cycle, leaving operators facing significantly higher debt service costs to stay in business, St. Juste said. Nontraded SFR REIT VineBrook Homes Trust suspended share buybacks earlier this month after ending a tender offer that drew three times as many shares as the REIT sought to buy. VineBrook, which has 20,500 units in 21 states, flagged an upcoming $650.8M debt maturity within a year as a driving factor behind the shift in strategy. For Invitation Homes and American Homes 4 Rent , the two biggest publicly traded single-family rental firms, the legislation creates a unique and sizable rollup opportunity, St. Juste wrote in a September analysis. The two REITs have trailed the broader REIT index by about 13 percentage points this year, according to Mizuho’s September report, and investors see upside potential in the wide gap that exists between the firms’ public valuations and the value of the properties in their portfolios. The REITs have been using that gap to sell homes and buy back stock at an attractive valuation, a trend that is expected to continue into 2027. items.title: Fitch warns of growing balance-sheet strain at top nonbank mortgage firms
items.description: Fitch Ratings revised its outlooks on three major nonbank mortgage companies to negative and warned that elevated leverage and growing mortgage servicing rights (MSR) exposure are weighing on credit profiles in a higher-for-longer rate environment. In a periodic review of nine publicly rated nonbank mortgage firms released Monday, Fitch affirmed all long-term issuer default ratings but shifted the outlooks for Pennymac Financial Services , Planet Financial Group and Freedom Mortgage Holdings to negative from stable. Fitch maintained the following long-term issuer default ratings: Onity Group at B-, UWM Holdings Corp. at B+, Pennymac at BB, Planet at B, CrossCountry Mortgage at BB-, Rocket Companies at BBB-, Freedom at BB-, Finance of America at CCC and Provident Funding Associates at B. Fitch said profitability for several lenders is likely to be constrained in 2027, given a challenging rate backdrop that limits refinance volume and makes it harder for companies to retain earnings and pay down debt . That dynamic is expected to pressure leverage ratios across the sector. Three negative outlooks At Pennymac , corporate leverage has exceeded Fitch’s 1.5x downgrade trigger since the first quarter of 2026. And a failure to make meaningful progress toward reducing corporate leverage to 1.5x or less over the outlook horizon could lead to a downgrade to BB-, Fitch said. “Fitch expects profitability to be constrained in 2027 by a challenging rate environment and the lag in realizing the full impact of recent expense reduction initiatives,” Fitch stated. For Planet , the agency pointed to a significant increase in MSR exposure since 2021, as the company retained servicing from its own originations and acquired bulk portfolios. MSRs represented about 363% of company equity in the second quarter of 2026, up from 293% a year earlier and above the level of higher-rated peers, Fitch said. Planet’s corporate leverage also rose to 5.5x, up from 4.3x during the same period. Fitch considers that level high and a key constraint on the rating. The agency said it could downgrade Planet if leverage rises above its 7.0x trigger. At Freedom , corporate leverage — measured as gross nonfunding debt to tangible equity — reached Fitch’s 2.0x downgrade trigger in the second quarter, up from 1.9x at the end of 2025. Shareholder distributions exceeded earnings in the first half of the year, contributing to the increase. Fitch expects Freedom’s leverage to rise further as it grows its servicing portfolio and uses available borrowing capacity to meet potential margin calls under its hedging program. A closer look at top lenders At UWM , Fitch cited high leverage, MSR valuation risk and reliance on short-term, largely uncommitted secured funding as constraints on its rating. Corporate leverage, excluding origination funding, climbed to 5.3x in the third quarter of 2026, nearly double the 2.7x figure at the end of 2025. MSR mark-to-market volatility and a $603 million hedge loss in the second quarter have weighed on profitability. Still, Fitch pointed to a 30% adjusted EBITDA margin for the trailing 12 months through the third quarter as evidence of solid core earnings. “Fitch expects leverage to decline over time, supported by planned MSR sales and earnings above the expected $165 million annual preferred dividend. Common dividends are suspended. Even so, Fitch expects corporate leverage to remain above 2.0x over the Outlook horizon.” Regarding CCM, its acquisition of Two Harbors Investment Corp. brought $156 billion in unpaid principal balance to its servicing portfolio, along with the RoundPoint Mortgage Servicing platform’s in-house capabilities. Fitch expects the added scale and greater retention of servicing economics to improve profitability, although it does not anticipate the full integration benefits until the end of 2028. The acquisitions also drove up leverage. Corporate leverage rose to 2.9x, up from 1.2x and above Fitch’s 2.0x rating sensitivity. Fitch expects CCM to reduce leverage toward its 1.0x corporate target. Failure to bring leverage below downgrade triggers within 12 to 24 months could result in a negative rating action. At Rocket , corporate leverage stood at 1.1x in the third quarter, down from 1.4x at the end of 2025 but above the 0.5x recorded at the end of 2024, before its acquisitions of Redfin and Mr. Cooper Group . Although Rocket remains above Fitch’s 1.0x downgrade trigger, the agency expects leverage to fall below that level over the next 12 months through repayment of secured borrowings and moderate earnings retention. The pace will depend on market conditions and whether the company realizes the expected acquisition synergies, Fitch said. Related More: Fitch Ratings MSRs PennyMac Rocket Companies

items.description: Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October, According to NAR Report Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More November 18, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Residential Real Estate , Promoting Home Ownership , Financing & Credit , Mortgages & Home Financing Share Month-Over-Month 4.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions Year-Over-Year 16.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions WASHINGTON (November 18, 2026) – Pending home sales in October decreased by 4.7% month-over-month and 16.7% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS ® Pending Home Sales report . The report helps the real estate ecosystem—including agents, homebuyers and sellers—better understand the housing market by providing data on the level of home sales under contract. Month-over-month pending home sales declined in all four major U.S. regions. Year-over-year pending home sales also declined in all four regions. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” October 2026 National Pending Home Sales 4.7% decrease month-over-month 16.7% decrease year-over-year October 2026 Regional Pending Home Sales Northeast 0.8% decrease month-over-month 11.1% decrease year-over-year Midwest 2.7% decrease month-over-month 14.0% decrease year-over-year South 6.3% decrease month-over-month 18.7% decrease year-over-year West 6.9% decrease month-over-month 20.3% decrease year-over-year At the local level, pending home sales fell year-over-year even in the strongest markets. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the following 10 markets posted the smallest annual declines in pending home sales, according to data from Realtor.com ® Economics: Cincinnati, OH-KY-IN (-4.7%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-9.7%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-10.0%) Indianapolis-Carmel-Greenwood, IN (-11.3%) Chicago-Naperville-Elgin, IL-IN (-11.9%) Pittsburgh, PA (-12.4%) Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (-12.7%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, NY (-12.7%) Jacksonville, FL (-12.8%) Cleveland, OH (-12.8%) About the National Association of REALTORS ® The National Association of REALTORS ® is involved in all aspects of residential and commercial real estate. The term REALTOR ® is a registered collective membership mark that identifies a real estate professional who is a member of the National Association of REALTORS ® and subscribes to its strict Code of Ethics . For free consumer guides about navigating the homebuying and selling transaction processes—from written buyer agreements to negotiating compensation—visit facts.realtor . # # # The Pending Home Sales Index is a leading indicator for the housing sector, based on pending sales of existing homes. A sale is listed as pending when the contract has been signed but the transaction has not closed, though the sale usually is finalized within one or two months of signing. Pending contracts are good early indicators of upcoming sales closings. However, the amount of time between pending contracts and completed sales is not identical for all home sales. Variations in the length of the process from pending contract to closed sale can be caused by issues such as buyer difficulties with obtaining mortgage financing, home inspection problems, or appraisal issues. The index is based on a sample that covers about 40% of multiple listing service data each month. In developing the model for the index, it was demonstrated that the level of monthly sales-contract activity parallels the level of closed existing-home sales in the following two months. An index of 100 is equal to the average level of contract activity during 2001, which was the first year to be examined. By coincidence, the volume of existing-home sales in 2001 fell within the range of 5.0 to 5.5 million, which is considered normal for the current U.S. population. items.title: Sherwood Equities Sells Hudson Yards Development Site For $100M: The N.Y. Deal Sheet
items.description: Long before Hudson Yards was the buzzy hot spot it is today, Sherwood Equities snapped up a 17K SF parcel of land at 460 10th Ave. And this week, it sold it to Joyland Group for $100M, Commercial Observer first reported . Google Maps The site at 460 10th Ave. is now slated to become housing. Sherwood had owned the residential development site since the 1990s, according to the firm’s website . It is unclear why Sherwood sold the property, but it once had plans to build more than 200 apartments on the site, according to The Real Deal . As recently as February, Sherwood agreed to add affordable housing to the site and invest $11.8M in neighborhood infrastructure upgrades in exchange for tacking on another 70K SF to the development, according to plans filed with the Department of Buildings. Now, a partnership between Joyland and Prospect Development has big plans for the site, Commercial Observer reported. The duo wants to build a 34-story, 456-unit apartment building. JLL’s Jonathan Hageman, Ethan Stanton, Andrew Scandalios, Hall Oster, Michael Mazzara and Brendan Maddigan represented Sherwood in the sale. The property had been on the market for a little over a year, according to an announcement on the brokerage’s website. TOP SALES Tishman Realty sold a 50K SF parking garage at 112 E. 16th St. to Pro-H Development for $44.3M, Crain's New York Business reported . The garage, which sits between Irving Place and Union Square East, will likely be demolished to make way for housing. Tishman representatives had filed permits to build a 22-story, 52-unit mixed-use building before the sale, with the new owner planning to turn the 52 units into for-sale homes. *** Trammell Crow Co. acquired 442 W. 18th St., a lot with a vacant two-story garage and office building, for $67.5M, PincusCo reported . The seller was family-owned Retaco Holding, which had owned the site since 1983. The new owner plans to build a 14-story mixed-use residential and commercial building. JLL’s Jonathan Hageman, Steven Rutman and Tyler Peck worked with Institutional Property Advisors’ Steven Siegel and Eric Anton to arrange the off-market deal for Retaco, Commercial Observer reported . *** Namdar Realty Group and Mason Asset Management snagged a 132K SF office building at 71 Fifth Ave. for $60.6M, PincusCo reported . Namdar and Mason borrowed $42M from Truist Bank to finance the purchase. The sellers were Madison Capital and Lubert-Adler. TOP LEASES Google Maps GFP's 520 Eighth Ave., where the Mason Tenders’ District Council Trust Funds is staying put for another 10 years Mason Tenders’ District Council Trust Funds renewed its 40K SF lease at GFP Real Estate’s 520 Eighth Ave. for another 10 years, according to a release. The organization has been in the 1926-built, 860K SF building since 2001 and plans to continue to use the property as its administrative offices. GFP’s Matthew Mandell handled the transaction in-house without any outside brokerages. *** MD Squared Property Group leased 16K SF at The Feil Organization’s 145 W. 30th St., bringing the property to 100% leased, according to a release. The deal follows Feil’s announcement that Turner School had renewed its 8K SF lease on the sixth floor of the 12-story office. Andrew Wiener represented the landlord in-house, while MD Squared represented itself. *** Nonprofit Child Center of NY inked a 16K SF lease at Stellar Management’s 35-01 36th Ave. in Astoria, Commercial Observer reported . Asking rents for the 10-year deal at the nine-story building were $50 per SF. Sholom & Zuckerbrot’s Gail Roseman represented the tenant, while NY Space Finders’ Luca DiCiero and Faisal Gilani represented the landlord. Coworking firm International Workplace Group, which signed for 8K SF in January 2025, is the building’s anchor. *** Activate Games signed a 16K SF lease at Acadia Realty Trust’s Downtown Brooklyn mall, City Point, Crain’s New York Business reported . The live-action video game experience company will occupy a ground-floor, mezzanine and lower-level space. The store is expected to open in June. Momentum Realty Group’s Chandler Slate represented the tenant. TOP FINANCING Google Maps 21-12 30th Road in Astoria, where Mega Contracting Group scored a $256.3M loan to develop hundreds of homes Mega Contracting Group scored a $256.3M construction loan for a 236-unit mixed-use project at 21-12 30th Road in Astoria, PincusCo reported . The funding came from a group of lenders including TD Bank, Enterprise Community Partners, NYC Department of Housing Preservation and Development and the NYS Housing Finance Agency. The property has an alternative address of 30-37 21st St. *** Wells Fargo provided a $258.2M loan to L+M Development Partners to refinance three apartment buildings in East Harlem, PincusCo reported . The properties span 1M SF across 761 units. They are located at 1962 and 1940 First Ave. and 455 E. 102nd St. The debt retires a $232.1M Fannie Mae loan. *** Artifact and Ashok Khuban netted two refinancing loans totaling $147.5M and covering three rental buildings in Upper Manhattan, PincusCo reported . Bank of Montreal provided the financing. The first loan, valued at $94M, was for 636-646 W. 158th St. and retires a $85.5M sum. The second loan, a $53.5M sum, was for 1871-1873 and 1867 Amsterdam Ave. and replaces a $46.2M sum. The prior lender in both cases was Genesis Capital. items.title: New Home Lot Supply Index
items.description: New Home Lot Supply Index The New Home Lot Supply Index provides an unrivaled look into the lot markets across the country, offering a current quarter snapshot as well as insight into the directional trend. This report details data for the third quarter of 2026. November 18, 2026 – 4 min read Table of Content: Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index (LSI) for 3Q26, rose for the ninth consecutive quarter and showed lot supply loosened both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter across the United States. The index is a residential real estate indicator based on the number of single-family vacant developed lots (VDL) and the rate at which those lots are absorbed via housing starts. The New Home LSI came in at 88.5 for 3Q26, representing a 20.8% increase from 3Q25. This quarter, the market continued to be rated “appropriately supplied.” On a quarter-over-quarter basis, supply increased by 3.9% from 2Q26. The LSI counts the total vacant developed lot supply and adjusts it for overall starts activity. “The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” said Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market. Affordability pressures and widespread incentives underscore the challenges builders face in converting demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market means availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction; it does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost challenges have disappeared.” In 2Q26, the LSI sat right on the boundary between "slightly undersupplied" and "appropriately supplied." However, the upward movement in Q3 solidified the national rating as “appropriately supplied.” In 3Q26, lot supply loosened year-over-year across all major metropolitan areas Zonda tracks, except Boise. For markets that saw an increase in lot supply, the average year-over-year gain was significant at +32%. More markets trended up and were rated “appropriately supplied” or “oversupplied” in the third quarter, but 12 out of 30 were still categorized as “significantly undersupplied.” The markets where land supply loosened the most on a year-over-year basis were Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle. Boise was the only market where local lot supply tightened compared to 3Q25, falling from 65.7 to 51.9, joining one of 12 markets rated “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed ratings this quarter, as outlined in the chart below: Zonda also records future lots through the stages of development. The stages range from raw land through streets in, which is the last step before the lot becomes a vacant developed lot. Zonda groups the last few stages into a classification called total upcoming lots, which typically indicates delivery over the next 12-18 months. Total upcoming lots in 3Q26 increased 1.0% year-over-year and 1.6% quarter-over-quarter. These types of lots in the third quarter were down 12.2% from the 2022 peak but were up 23.4% compared to the same quarter in 2019. Among total upcoming lots, roadwork was down 15.3% year-over-year. Roadwork is comprised of the two smaller stages—streets paved and streets in—and represents the last step in lot development. Lots in the excavation stage were up 8.6% year-over-year, and those with equipment on site were up 5.7%. The largest share of total upcoming lots were in the excavation stage in 3Q26, totaling 416K. These lots have an expected delivery between 2Q27 and 3Q27 (the range represents different timeframes from local entitlement processes). Note, not all of the lots in excavation will match Zonda’s estimated timeline. “The development pipeline is edging higher, but the mix of activity matters,” Fergus said. “More lots are in excavation and equipment-on-site stages than a year ago, while fewer are in the final roadwork stages. That points to continued investment in future communities, but an uneven flow of near-term deliveries. Builders will need to weigh today’s softer demand environment against the time required to prepare lots for future construction.” Get a first look at Land AI Get a first look at Zonda Land AI on December 10th. items.title: HUD finalizes rule targeting mixed-immigration-status households receiving aid
items.description: HUD finalizes rule targeting mixed-immigration-status households receiving aid The rule could displace tens of thousands of people, housing organizations say. A lawsuit claims the change is illegal and unconstitutional. Published Nov. 18, 2026 Ryan Kushner Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google A U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule finalized Nov. 12, 2026, requires tenants receiving federal housing assistance to provide proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status for all household members. Getty Images First published on Listen to the article 2 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Dive Brief: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development finalized a rule Nov. 12 requiring households receiving federal housing assistance to provide proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status for all household members. The rule, which goes into effect Dec. 14, effectively ends prorated federal housing assistance, which based the level of assistance on the number of eligible family members in the household. The new regulation could impact housing assistance for as many as 80,000 people, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A lawsuit challenging the rule’s legality was filed in the U.S. Central District of California Monday. Dive Insight: Nearly 9 million people participate in HUD housing assistance programs, which have long required immigration eligibility, according to NLIHC. HUD said the rule aims to bolster the agency’s “enforcement of the law” by requiring verification of immigration status for all household residents. It asserts that providing assistance to mixed-status households reduces the funds available to households that are fully eligible. “It’s unacceptable that America’s homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner said Nov. 10 in a press release. The agency said an audit of HUD-assisted households found around 200,000 tenants “ with incomplete or unknown eligibility verification.” David Dworkin, president and CEO of the National Housing Conference, called the regulation “a step backward.” “HUD’s concerns about immigration should be addressed through enforcement of existing laws, not by effectively evicting families who are here legally and creating expensive and burdensome processes for housing providers that are not capable of immigration enforcement,” Dworkin said in a statement. Of the approximately 80,000 individuals who could be displaced by the new requirements, nearly half are children, according to NLIHC. The lawsuit was filed by three unnamed plaintiffs residing in public housing or receiving housing assistance in Los Angeles County and two Los Angeles-area housing advocacy groups. It alleges the rule violates the Fair Housing Act, the Administrative Procedures Act and the Constitution’s Fifth Amendment guarantee of due process rights. items.title: Fed Officials Expect Further Interest Rate Hikes After Pausing Last Month
items.description: Leaders at the Federal Reserve held firm on interest rates in October, but also felt a future rate hike "would likely be appropriate" as some mulled a larger hike in December, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. At the Oct. 27-28 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), policymakers voted 10-2 to keep the overnight rate at its previous 3.75%-4% range. The decision came days before the 2026 midterms, even as FOMC members agreed inflation was a persistent concern, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh joined the majority, while Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack , both voted in favor of a quarter-point increase. One month before, the FOMC voted to raise rates for the first time in three years in an effort to clamp down on inflation. The minutes—which don't name FOMC members specifically while discussing their deliberations—show that some of the FOMC members considered that, while the impact of tariffs on the economy was waning, high energy costs continue to pressure Americans. Indeed, some participants even noted that, if the inflation numbers got too unfavorable, they would consider a rate hike of more than a quarter-percent in December. Bond markets still view that as unlikely, with the probability of a larger half-point hike next month at just 5%, according to CME FedWatch . Still, Federal Reserve Gov. Christopher Waller told CNBC Wednesday it may be necessary to "shock people" with a larger rate hike. He said in a speech this month that a half-percent point hike might be necessary next month. "Inflation's been above our target for over five years, so if you really want to get it down you have to start taking more aggressive actions," Waller told CNBC. December rate hike looks all but certain FOMC members also said the rapid artificial intelligence buildout was contributing to inflation. But more scrutiny of the industry could slow spending and reduce inflation pressures. Those members later determined holding rates steady at the October meeting would allow for time to "assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, or geopolitical developments." "A couple of participants noted that, at the current juncture, a gradual approach to policy firming would give businesses and households time to adjust to higher interest rates," the minutes state. Inflation remained hot in October. Overall prices rose 0.4% from September , according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) last week. Some numbers look better. After a disappointing September , U.S. payrolls came roaring back in October as employers added 165,000 new jobs , pushing the unemployment rate down to 4.1%. CME FedWatch currently prices a roughly 95% chance of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raising the federal funds to a 4%-4.25% range in December, followed by a 69% probability of 4.25%-4.5% in January. The meeting minutes show that Fed leaders are aware that public sentiment broadly expects the December rate hike. "Some participants," the minutes state, judge those estimates to be "broadly consistent with their assessments of the appropriate policy rate path." Several of the meeting members also said it was a "close call." In the meantime, Cook and Hammack said that inflation remained too high and they didn't see enough signs that it was letting up. They worried that delaying the rate hike any further could risk higher inflation becoming entrenched. That, in turn, could mean more drastic rate hikes in the future. More rate hikes in the cards Waller isn't the only Fed leader saying that the market needs more than one quarter-point rate hike. "The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said this week at a conference in Argentina. Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said the market ultimately anticipates two or three hikes over the next 6 to 8 months. The Market has reacted. Pending home sales in September dropped to their lowest level on record . "While the market and the Fed both seem to agree that some monetary policy restriction is warranted, most investors currently expect more restriction than the Fed has projected," Hale said last month. But there is still an opportunity for homebuyers in this environment. Hale recommended homebuyers set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting credit, making a higher down payment, and shopping around for a mortgage. Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

items.title: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER
items.description: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER Single-family leasing activity increased as rental prices edged higher HOUSTON -- (November 18, 2026) -- Houston-area renters kept the market moving in October, leasing more homes than a year ago even as rental prices edged higher. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' October 2026 Rental Market Update, 3,850 single-family homes were leased, a 3.5% increase from 3,720 in October 2025. A healthy supply of rental homes helped keep prices relatively stable. The average lease price for a single-family home rose just 1.2% to $2,293, compared to $2,266 in October 2025. "With affordability still top of mind, many people are taking a closer look at their housing options and what works best for their budgets," said HAR Chair-Elect Kat Robinson with SERHANT. "As we head toward the end of the year, that will continue to play a big role in whether people decide to rent or buy. For renters, it's encouraging to see that prices haven't changed much from last year." Townhomes and condominiums also saw an increase in leasing activity. A total of 638 properties were leased in October, up 9.1% from 585 a year earlier. The average lease price rose 4.0% to $1,943, while the median price increased 2.9% to $1,800. Rental inventory in this segment continued to expand. New listings increased 1.7% to 1,143 properties, while active listings rose 3.3% to 2,387. Townhomes and condominiums spent an average of 48 days on the market, one day longer than a year ago. Life sciences in the local region partially thrives from funding to universities from the National Institutes of Health (NIH); in the third quarter, Stanford ranked eighth while UCSF took the second spot, based on dollars awarded nationally. Venture capital funding into Bay Area life sciences companies in the third quarter came in at $2.1 billion, according to Pitchbook. The largest deals in the region went to San Francisco-based Chai Discovery at $400.0 million and South San Francisco-based Encoded at $275.0 million. Supply & Demand: Rising Vacancy in the East Bay The overall vacancy rate at the end of the third quarter of 2026 was 28.5%, down 20 basis points (bps) from 28.7% in the previous quarter and down 60 bps from 29.1% one year ago. Direct vacancy stayed relatively flat around 11.5 million square feet (msf). Sublease vacancy was consistent quarter-over-quarter as well at 2.5 msf. East Bay Oakland vacancy increased the most year-over-year, up 230 bps or 255,104 square feet (sf) from the same quarter last year, largely due to the delivery of new construction projects that completed in 2025. Additional consolidations also contributed to vacancy over the last 18 months. There was 828,511 sf of total leasing activity (new leases and renewals) for the third quarter, an increase from the 748,556 sf in the second quarter, and up from 783,364 sf during the same period last year. New leases made up 75.4% or 624,859 sf of the activity, while renewals made up the rest at 24.6% or 203,652 sf. New leases with Lilly Gateway Labs (South San Francisco) and Structure Therapeutics (South San Francisco) contributed significantly to activity this quarter. Supply: Eight Large-Scale Projects Completed in 2025 & 2026 There were eight ground-up developments, all speculative and totaling approximately 2.0 msf, completed since the beginning of 2025. These included Avia Labs (315,000 sf) in Millbrae, SPUR Phase I (330,350 sf) in South San Francisco, and The Landing (503,500 sf) in Burlingame. Along with those were 1030 Brittan Ave (108,134 sf) in San Carlos which was preleased to MBC Biolabs in 2022, Portal 405 (240,000 sf) in San Carlos, Menlo Park Labs (268,468 sf), and 200 Twin Dolphin (234,000 sf) in Redwood Shores. Finally, the last project that completed construction was ELCO Yards – The Shop in Redwood City, totaling 225,878 sf. Conversions were more active in the Bay Area in the third quarter with roughly 336,433 sf in the pipeline. Projects under renovation are 2400-2470 Charleston Road (108,474 sf) in Mountain View, Island Parkway (179,172 sf) in Redwood Shores, and 901 California Avenue (54,800 sf) in Palo Alto. Overall average asking rates have been steadily decreasing in in the Santa Clara County and San Mateo County markets with the former having the largest change from $4.58 psf in the second quarter of 2026 to $4.32 psf in the third quarter. San Francisco County recorded a quarterly increase to its average asking rates due to several higher-end spaces that came to market including 1700 Owens Street. items.title: Congress Puts Up $216M For Energy Department Relocation From Forrestal
items.description: The Department of Energy’s 1.8M SF office complex along Independence Avenue is one step closer to its next chapter. A Senate committee approved $215.6M in funding Wednesday to relocate the agency’s employees from the James V. Forrestal trio of office buildings into its next headquarters. The funds can be used to prepare Forrestal for disposition and Energy's new headquarters for its habitation, according to a resolution from the Senate’s Environment and Public Works Committee. The 1960s-era Forrestal complex at 1000 Independence Ave. SW acts as a massive physical barrier between the National Mall and the Wharf. Its redevelopment has long been viewed by urban planners as a key component in unlocking a mixed-use vision for D.C.'s southwest federal corridor. Google Maps The Department of Energy's James V. Forrestal Building at 1000 Independence Ave. SW The funding will go to the federal government’s landlord, the General Services Administration , via its FY2026 Optimization Program Prospectus. The EPW Committee passed that prospectus Wednesday, and a House panel approved the funding in July . The GSA announced in March that Energy would be clearing out of Forrestal and moving into the Department of Education’s 50-year-old headquarters: the Lyndon B. Johnson Building on Maryland Avenue Southwest. Education, in turn, announced that it would move into a building at 500 D St. SW, which was previously leased for the now largely defunct U.S. Agency for International Development. That move, expected to cut Education's footprint by 80%, was set to be completed in August. The GSA said in a Wednesday news release that the relocation money allows the agency “to consider alternative uses for the Forrestal Building, including disposition.” The GSA didn’t provide a timeline for when the move will begin or how long it should take. Its press office didn’t respond to Bisnow ’s request for information. GSA Administrator Edward Forst said in the release that the move will “reduce waste, avoid more than $350 million in delinquent maintenance costs, and deliver a workplace that better serves agencies, employees, and the American taxpayer.” In September, a Government Accountability Office report said the agency would need funding to “fit out classified space to meet Energy’s mission needs” at its new LBJ Building home. Momentum has been building over the past two years to transform the 230 acres that make up D.C.’s southwest federal corridor into a new mixed-use neighborhood. The federal government this year offloaded its first two federal properties in the corridor : the Regional Office Building and the Liberty Loan Building on the Tidal Basin. It has earmarked other large headquarters buildings for disposition but this summer seemed to quietly pull back on those efforts, the Washington Business Journal reported . Public and private stakeholders have worried about the lack of a coherent vision and plan for the neighborhood. The first sign that a formal planning document was underway came last month when Diane Sullivan, the acting executive director of the National Capital Planning Commission, presented a preliminary vision for the neighborhood, broken into three districts, each with a distinct focus: residential, arts and culture, and federal office. Under that vision, Forrestal, which sits across from the Smithsonian’s Arts and Industries Building, would be included in the 10th Street Cultural/Entertainment District. items.title: Kisco Senior Living Lands $52M Refi on San Rafael Senior Living Community
items.description: California CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. California + Bay Area + Senior Housing | November 18, 2026 By: Allen Wolfsheimer Kisco Senior Living Lands $52M Refi on San Rafael Senior Living Community Kisco Senior Living has obtained a $52.2 million Freddie Mac refinance loan on Drake Terrace, a 123-unit senior living community in San Rafael the firm has owned since 2001. The property is located at 275 Los Ranchitos Road in the city’s Terra Linda neighborhood, roughly 22 miles north of San Francisco. Drake Terrace has maintained occupancy above 91% throughout the past 24 months. The community was originally developed in 1989 and offers independent and assisted living, in addition to memory care, allowing residents to transition between care levels on-site. Resident amenities include all-day chef-driven dining, a fitness center, raised garden beds, courtyards, a library and scheduled transportation. Chris Cain , Tyler Armstrong , and Taylor Russ with Lument arranged the 10-year loan, which features a fixed-rate term with full-term interest-only payments. The loan refinances existing Freddie Mac debt and provides cash-out proceeds. Cain and Lument previously worked with Kisco on the financing of Park Terrace, a 230-bed, resort-style senior living community in Rancho Santa Margarita, which closed in May 2025. items.title: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook
items.description: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook Written by Kenny Lee on November 18, 2026 What happened Housing starts jumped 9.9% from September to 1.309 million SAAR in October, up 2.8% from September last year. While starts in the West fell to the lowest in more than six years, the Midwest and South showed strength, rising 48.4% and 10.5%, respectively. However, sharp declines in new-construction permits indicate builders’ caution. Authorized units declined 7.4% to 1.295 million in October, with the single-family segment down sharply by 8.7%. All four Census regions saw declines in single-family construction permits. While notoriously volatile, multifamily housing starts nationwide jumped 25.5% to 433 thousand units in October. Although multifamily permits fell 5.2% from September to 475 thousand units in October, the latest pace is an improvement from this summer. Compared to last year, the three-month moving average of multifamily permits was up 3.5% from a year ago. Why it matters Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October , the largest year-over-year drop since 2023. Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes , the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane. The flipside of cooling buyer demand is skyrocketing renter demand. As elevated borrowing costs push would-be buyers to rent instead, renter demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Although the industry has been grappling with high new construction inventory over the past few years since the construction boom in 2022 and 2023, recent Zillow data shows market fundamentals started improving this year. The typical multifamily rent increased 2.5% year over year in October, compared to 1.3% growth one year ago, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. Stronger rent growth reflects a resurgence of renter demand across the country. Recent gains in multifamily permits could be an early sign that the supply outlook is transitioning to growth. That said, it is worth noting that the Census Bureau's multifamily construction data relies on a survey with a small sample and is often subject to large revisions, and it will take additional data to see whether the recent gains indicate a new trend. Although developers still face challenging market conditions, such as high costs of construction financing, building materials, and skilled labor, a sustained improvement in multifamily supply will help alleviate the pressure on renters. items.title: Homeownership Remains a Key to Household Wealth
items.description: Homeownership Remains a Key to Household Wealth November 18, 2026 Jing Fu No Comments Homeownership continues to play an important role for household wealth accumulation in the United States. Beyond providing stability, owning a home allows households to build equity over time and accumulate a valuable financial asset. As highlighted in a previous blog post , the benefits of homeownership extend beyond wealth accumulation to include greater financial security, retirement stability, and broader household and community well-being. The latest Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances ( SCF ) 1 underscores the importance of housing in household finances. In 2025, primary residences accounted for more than one-quarter of total household assets, with an aggregate value of $47.2 trillion. The data also reveal a substantial wealth gap between homeowners and renters and show how important home equity varies across income and age groups. Primary Residences Remain an Important Household Asset Primary residences represent one of the largest components of U.S. household assets, exceeding several major financial and investment asset categories (Figure 1). In 2025, the aggregate value of primary residences reached $47.2 trillion, accounting for 26% of total household assets. This exceeded the value of other financial assets 2 (20%, or $36.3 trillion), retirement accounts (18%, or $33.4 trillion), and business interests (17%, or $31.5 trillion). Homeownership is also widely distributed among U.S. households. Nearly two-thirds (66%) owned their primary residence in 2025. By comparison, 55% of households held retirement accounts, while 20% owned stocks or bonds. Although other financial assets were held by 99% of households, this broad category includes checking accounts, money market accounts, and prepaid debit cards, which are often used primarily for everyday financial transactions rather than long-term wealth accumulation. The substantial share of household assets represented by primary residences highlights the importance of housing in the overall financial well-being of American households. Homeowners Continue to be Wealthier than Renters The importance of housing as a household asset is also reflected in the substantial wealth difference between homeowners and renters (Figure 2). In 2025, the median net worth of homeowner households was $458,900, compared with just $10,600 for renter households. This means that the median homeowner household had approximately 43 times the net worth of the median renter household. Between 2022 and 2025, median net worth among homeowners increased by 6%, while renters’ median net worth declined by 7%. The wealth gap extends beyond home equity. Homeowners also tend to hold greater amounts of financial assets, including retirement accounts, stocks, and other investments. In 2025, median financial assets among homeowners who held financial assets were $109,800, compared with $5,300 among renters who held financial assets. This difference suggests that the wealth advantage associated with homeownership is reflected in broader household balance sheets, not just housing wealth. It is worth noting that income, age, education, and other household characteristics also contribute to the observed wealth gap. These findings therefore illustrate the strong association between homeownership and greater household wealth rather than establishing homeownership as the sole cause of the difference. Beyond providing stability, owning a home allows households to build equity over time and accumulate a valuable financial asset.
